Base directory for this skill: /workspaces/ai-agent-llms/.claude/skills/simplified-technical-english

# Simplified Technical English

## Overview

A writing contract adapted from ASD-STE-100, the controlled-English standard used for
aerospace and defence maintenance manuals. It exists because a reader who misreads a
procedure breaks something expensive.

**Core principle: one instruction, one sentence, one meaning.**

The output is judged by shape, not by taste. A sentence either fits the contract or it
does not, and you can measure that.

## When to Use

- Procedures, runbooks, migration steps, incident playbooks
- Warnings, cautions, error messages
- API docs and reference material read under time pressure
- Any document whose readers include non-native English speakers
- A reader has already misread the document once

**Do not use for:**

- Prose that must persuade or entertain
- Commit messages — use conventional-commit style
- Narrative design docs, where nuance beats speed

## The Contract

Write each sentence to satisfy all nine:

| # | Rule | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One instruction per sentence | 1 |
| 2 | Procedure sentence length | ≤ 20 words |
| 3 | Descriptive sentence length | ≤ 25 words |
| 4 | Paragraph length, one topic each | ≤ 6 sentences |
| 5 | Noun cluster length | ≤ 3 nouns |
| 6 | Start an instruction with its verb | imperative |
| 7 | Use the same word for the same thing | 1 word = 1 meaning |
| 8 | Keep articles: *the*, *a*, *an* | always |
| 9 | Use simple tenses: past, present, future | no perfect/progressive |

In a warning, put the condition first. Put the command second.
**"If the cache is cold, fetch the blobs before you check out."**

## Rewrite Patterns

Each pattern shows a real sentence and its replacement.

**Split on the conjunction.** One clause becomes one sentence.

> The bug is silent in the configuration the project has always used, and loud in the one
> it had never successfully run — because `response_only` was independently broken until
> `bac1d98`. *(41 words)*

> The bug is silent in the usual configuration. It is loud in cell C2. Only C2 uses
> `response_only`. Commit `bac1d98` fixed `response_only`. *(8 / 5 / 4 / 5 words)*

**Name the actor.** Passive hides who acts.

> The collator is truncated to 1024 tokens. → TRL truncates every batch to 1024 tokens.

**Repeat the noun.** A pronoun two sentences from its noun is a guess.

> It overwrites it. → The C2 run overwrites the C0 checkpoint.

**Unstack the nouns.** Break clusters longer than three.

> Cat A SFT corpus role corruption fix → the fix for corrupted roles in the Cat A corpus

**Lift steps into a list.** A sentence with three commas is a list in disguise.

> Run the cleaner, then split the corpus, then filter the prompts, and push the result.

> 1. Run the cleaner.
> 2. Split the corpus.
> 3. Filter the prompts.
> 4. Push the result.

## One Word, One Meaning

Choose one term per concept and keep it for the whole document.

| Keep | Drop |
|---|---|
| start | launch, kick off, fire off, spin up |
| delete | remove, drop, purge, clear |
| fix | resolve, address, handle, sort out |
| check | verify, validate, confirm, ensure |
| fail | break, blow up, die, choke |

Write the list at the top of a long document. Follow it.

## Verify

Do not judge by feel. Measure:

```bash
python check_ste.py path/to/doc.md
```

It reports sentence count, mean and maximum length, the share over 20 words, and the
passive-voice share. It prints every sentence that breaks the contract, so you can fix
them one at a time.

**Gate:** no sentence over 25 words, and under 10% of sentences over 20 words.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Em dashes joining two full clauses | Make them two sentences. |
| A parenthesis carrying a second instruction | Give it its own sentence or a footnote. |
| "This" with no noun after it | Name the thing: "this failure", "this file". |
| Hedges: *should*, *might*, *typically* | State the condition: "If X, then Y." |
| A 30-word bullet | A bullet obeys the same 20-word limit. |
| Rewriting a quotation to fit | Quote exactly. The contract covers your words. |

## Real-World Impact

Three technical documents were measured in one repository, before any rewrite.
Between 33% and 46% of their sentences ran over 20 words. The longest reached 47.
The split and actor patterns moved a section under the gate. No fact was lost.

=== dc84adb11abe928abfdf9dcc1b8a8d580ec0ca62 chore(dvc): record mined model negatives (51 of 399 prompts, 12.8% error rate) ===
Yield by fault type, from greedy decoding on TRAIN prompts with C2 checkpoint-1767:

  model_wrong_args      19
  model_state_error     17
  model_no_tool_call    15

295 generations matched gold on every scored axis and 53 were byte-identical to
it, so both were dropped rather than emitted as zero-margin pairs.

The 12.8% error rate is well below the ~30% predicted from the held-out audit
(38.0% wrong on tool-bearing rows). Two candidate explanations, neither yet
tested: the audit set is v2 test data while these prompts are v2 train, which
the checkpoint saw during SFT; and the audit scores a stricter composite than
this classifier, which only flags a row when the tool name, arguments or state
annotation actually disagree.

  out  data/output/preference/task_a/model_negatives.jsonl
  1 file pushed to GCS; dvc status --cloud reports in sync.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

 1 file changed, 28 insertions(+)
=== de950ec607e31d4b8842c335d1466a45396b588b feat(data): mine on-distribution negatives; add DVC stages for the pair set ===
Adds scripts/mine_model_negatives.py and two DVC stages.

WHY MINED NEGATIVES. build_preference_pairs.py corrupts gold turns to make
negatives. R18 warns that synthetic-only negatives teach the model to
discriminate against the corruption function rather than to get the task right
— the same trap R15 documents at corpus level. The miner closes that gap: it
generates greedily from the checkpoint on TRAIN prompts, keeps the generations
that are actually wrong, and pairs each against its gold turn. Those negatives
are the mistakes the model really makes.

Selection is 75% tool-bearing on purpose. Greedy decoding is wrong on 38.0% of
tool-bearing rows versus 8.9% of no-tool rows, so the yield per GPU-minute is
far higher and lands on the current bottleneck (18 of 71 tool-bearing held-out
rows have the right tool and wrong arguments).

Failure types recorded per row: model_no_tool_call, model_wrong_tool,
model_wrong_args, model_state_error, model_other. Rows where the generation
matches gold on every scored axis are dropped — a zero-margin pair teaches that
the gold answer is also the bad one.

CONTAMINATION. The miner hard-refuses --split test and applies the same
prefix-fingerprint guard as the pair builder. The 206 held-out conversations are
the only contamination-free measuring stick for this lineage; mining negatives
from them and training on the result destroys it.

DVC STAGES.
  task_a_preference_pairs             synthetic pairs (CPU)
  task_a_preference_model_negatives   mined negatives (GPU, ~35 min for 400)

Outs are declared as FILES, not the directory. model_negatives.jsonl lives
beside train.jsonl/validation.jsonl, and a directory-level out would delete it
on every `dvc repro` of the synthetic stage.

The held-out set is documented as a prerequisite rather than a dep: it is
gitignored and rebuilt on demand from two git tags (cee970a), so it cannot be a
DVC dependency. Without it the stage fails loudly instead of silently skipping
the contamination guard.

Fixed en route: the miner passed rows keyed "prompt", but
_generate_for_checkpoint keys on "prompt_messages" (the shape _sample_prompts
emits). Failed at generation start, 20 s in, before any GPU work was wasted.

=== 165f2cc1ba3f0bed8d1d9a57af4d72b35523a111 feat(data): contrastive preference pair set for Cat A ===
R18 established that GRPO cannot learn here: the reward takes 11 distinct
values across 206 real completions and is exactly 1.0 on 81.1% of them, so
groups tie and the advantage is zero. Tool-bearing mix, trajectory aggregation
and higher temperature each moved the needle and none sufficed. A preference
objective sidesteps the problem — every pair carries a guaranteed margin, and
there is no generation in the loop, which matters when R9 forces HF rollouts at
~31 s/step.

Built: 29,256 train + 3,450 validation pairs in TRL conversational preference
format, from the v2-derived GRPO splits.

The three corruptions mirror failures C2 actually makes on held-out data rather
than invented ones:

  drop_tool_calls        announce-but-don't-call — narrates the action, emits no
                         <tool_call>. 9 of 71 tool-bearing rows.
  flip_state_transition  advances where the convention wants a self-loop, or the
                         reverse. Spurious self-loops: 26.9% in v4, 2.8% in C2.
  corrupt_tool_args      right tool, wrong arguments. 18 of 71 — the bottleneck.

Every corruption returns None when it cannot apply, so a pair whose `rejected`
equals its `chosen` cannot be emitted; a zero-margin pair actively teaches that
the gold answer is also the bad one.

BALANCE. First-applicable-corruption gave 76.9% flip_state_transition, because
flips apply to nearly every turn while both tool corruptions need a tool-bearing
one (~36% of rows). That over-weights the failure C2 has largely solved and
starves argument fidelity. Now every applicable corruption is generated and the
set is balanced to the scarcest type: 9,752 each, exactly 33.3%.

IN-DISTRIBUTION NEGATIVES. The first build produced `"Thai" -> "Thai_x"`. That
is the trap this work exists to avoid: the model would learn to reject an `_x`
suffix, scoring well on the pair set while being no better at the task — R15's
lesson at example level. Corruption now prefers a value-for-value swap between
two string arguments (nationality <-> trip_purpose), else a digit perturbation
that preserves identifier shape (CLM-55511 -> CLM-55521), else deletion of the
argument (missing-required-argument). No synthetic marker is ever introduced,
and a test asserts that across 25 seeds and 3 turn shapes.

CONTAMINATION GUARD — and a defect in my first version of it. The guard keyed
per-turn prompt fingerprints against whole-conversation fingerprints. A prompt
holds only the first k user turns, so those can never be equal: the guard was
INERT and passed everything while looking clean. Caught because the output
reported 15,688 "conversations" from a 2,558-conversation corpus.

Fixed with `user_turn_prefix_fingerprints`, which expands each excluded
conversation into all of its user-turn prefixes so a derived turn row really
matches. It now fires: 28 train + 5 validation rows excluded. Note it is
deliberately conservative — short prefixes can collide across conversations, so
a few exclusions are false positives. 33 rows of 32,706 is a cheap price for a
guard that works.

This matters because those 206 held-out conversations are the only
contamination-free measuring stick for the C2 lineage; training on them destroys
the ability to evaluate any of this. Independently re-verified at conversation
level: 0 overlap between the GRPO splits and the held-out set.

Negatives are SYNTHETIC. R18 recommends complementing them with negatives mined
from the model's own generations, which are on-distribution; every row carries
`source: "synthetic"` so the two can be distinguished once those exist. That
needs a generation pass over the TRAIN split — never the held-out set.

The 722 MB output is gitignored: it is a deterministic function of the
DVC-tracked GRPO splits plus this script and seed. A DVC stage for it is a
sensible follow-up, not done here.

Tests: tests/unit/test_preference_pairs.py (22, TDD - red first), including the
no-synthetic-marker property and two pinning that the contamination guard can
actually fire. Full suite 1455 passed.

=== 51624ee0d6b8accfac5e80ea356815c3d57241c1 docs(grpo): record the reward-resolution investigation and its negative result ===
Six commits of GRPO work today produced one durable finding: Cat A GRPO cannot
learn, because the reward has no resolution. Recording it before it evaporates,
together with the four defects found en route.

The optimizer is healthy — grad_norm 0.008-0.392 against a kill line of 50, KL
0.62-1.94 against 10, so the scale_rewards/dr_grpo/max_grad_norm stabilization
works. The reward is what fails: every step logged reward_std 0,
frac_reward_zero_std 1.

Not a reward bug. Scored directly it returns 1.0 / 0.0 / 0.44 on
perfect / bogus / unannotated completions. The prompt distribution saturates it:
63.9% of turns have no GT tool call, tool_call_f1([], []) == 1.0 gives them 0.40
free, and C2's 0.9369 state accuracy collects the rest — ~59% of prompts score
exactly 1.0. On 206 real completions the reward takes 11 distinct values, 81.1%
of them exactly 1.0.

Three independent attacks, all insufficient, which is why the recommendation is
to stop attacking it:
  - tool-bearing mix: informative-prompt share 19.4% -> 23.5% -> 29.3% -> 38.0%
  - trajectory mode: FAILS. At step 5, 8 of 8 genuinely distinct trajectories
    (lengths 77-113) scored identically. That kills both easy explanations and
    contradicts reward_business_logic_trajectory's own docstring claim.
  - temperature 0.8 -> 1.4: frac_reward_zero_std 1 -> 0, confirming the rollouts
    varied lexically not behaviourally, but reward_std only 0.00221-0.02283 — at
    or below the diagnostic's own "under-resolves" threshold, and bought by
    degrading the policy.

Recommended instead: preference learning (DPO/ORPO) on contrastive pairs, where
every pair carries a guaranteed margin and no reward variance is required. Two
constraints recorded because both are easy to get wrong: mine negatives from the
model's own errors rather than only synthetic corruptions (R15 showed a
structurally uniform edit gets learned as an unconditional habit), and never
source negatives from the held-out audit set or the only contamination-free
measuring stick for this lineage is gone.

Also records, in R18 and the doc:
  - the prompt_key collision (76 keys, 138 rows, 5.4%) whose mis-scoring would
    have INFLATED variance and biased the trajectory experiment toward a false
    pass;
  - that the R5 reward-hacking guardrail has been silently inactive on every
    Gemma-4 GRPO run, and is fixed but NOT yet independently confirmed;
  - the shared BatchEncoding normalization (suite 1391/5 -> 1433/0);
  - the expired VRAM geometry assumptions and the TRL max_prompt_length drop.

Two methodological notes are kept deliberately, because both nearly produced
wrong answers: cross-row reward std is the wrong statistic (GRPO cares about
variance across the N samples of one prompt), and an aggregation simulation over
independent rows is not evidence about a real multi-turn rollout.

No checkpoints from today are worth keeping: all three GRPO runs sit 2-4e-4
relative L2 from the C2 base they started from (max element delta ~5e-6), which
is what reward_std 0 predicts. Their value is the metrics, now written down.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

 docs/grpo_reward_resolution_investigation.md | 255 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++

=== 35bff48b254ad7b8c47396d66e32857614163340 test(grpo): exploration probe — trajectory rollout at temperature 1.4 ===
Isolates the one hypothesis left standing after 65cf697. That run measured, at
step 5, **8 of 8 genuinely distinct trajectories (lengths 77-113) all scoring
exactly the same reward**, with frac_reward_zero_std pinned at 1.0 across all
10 steps. Diversity was present and the reward still could not separate the
rollouts, which kills both easy explanations: the policy is not too
deterministic, and the per-turn discrete lattice is not the cause (that run WAS
the aggregated trajectory reward).

What is left: the trajectories may differ LEXICALLY rather than BEHAVIOURALLY —
same state path, same early stall, different wording — in which case the reward
is correctly reporting one outcome and the blocker is exploration, not reward
shaping.

Only two knobs move, so any change in reward_std is attributable to exploration
alone:

  temperature  0.8  -> 1.4
  top_p        0.95 -> 1.0   (do not re-truncate the widened tail)

Held fixed: C2 checkpoint, v2 data, num_generations 8, generation geometry,
optimizer settings, reward function, 10 steps. Separate output_dir so it cannot
resume onto the 0.8 run's trajectory (R13).

Reading the result:
  reward_std > 0     -> exploration is the lever; tune sampling, not the reward
  reward_std still 0 -> the reward components are genuinely too coarse and need
                        finer within-turn credit; temperature cannot help, and
                        that is a much larger piece of work

RESULT PENDING — the run is in flight and has not logged a step at commit time.
Committing the probe config so the experiment is reproducible regardless of how
it lands; the finding will follow separately. Neither mode is cleared for a
1000-step run: both currently sit at frac_reward_zero_std 1.0.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

scripts/build_preference_pairs.py:2:"""Build the Cat A contrastive preference pair set (DPO/ORPO format).
---
---configs/training---
grpo_cat_a.yaml
grpo_cat_a_c2_diagnostic.yaml
grpo_cat_a_c2_trajectory.yaml
grpo_cat_a_c2_trajectory_temp.yaml
grpo_cat_a_diagnostic.yaml
grpo_cat_b.yaml
grpo_cat_c.yaml
sft_cat_a.yaml
sft_cat_a_c2.yaml
sft_cat_b.yaml
sft_cat_c.yaml
---tail of investigation doc---
**Stop trying to extract variance from this reward.** Three independent attempts — richer prompt mix
(§4), trajectory aggregation (§5), higher temperature (§5.1) — each moved the needle a little and
none produced a usable learning signal. The common cause is that the reward is a coarse, quantized
function of a workflow outcome, and a strongly-SFT'd policy nearly always produces the *same*
outcome with different words.

**Use preference learning instead.** The failure modes are already measured per row on the held-out
audit, and they map directly onto contrastive pairs:

- **chosen** — the gold assistant turn (correct `[STATE: X → Y]`, correct tool call)
- **rejected** — the same turn corrupted in a way C2 actually fails:
  - narrates the action but emits no `<tool_call>` (the announce-but-don't-call gap)
  - advances the state where the convention wants a self-loop, or vice versa
  - right tool name, wrong arguments — **18 of 71** tool-bearing rows, the current bottleneck

This needs no reward variance at all: every pair carries a guaranteed margin. DPO/ORPO is also
cheaper per step than GRPO here, because there is no generation in the loop — which matters
given R9 forces HF `generate()` rollouts on Gemma-4 (~31 s/step).

**Two constraints on building it:**

1. **Mine negatives from the model's own errors, not only synthetic corruptions.** Synthetic
   negatives teach the model to discriminate against *your corruption function*; its real errors are
   on-distribution and teach it to discriminate against itself. R15 is the cautionary precedent — a
   structurally uniform edit got learned as an unconditional habit.
2. **Never source negatives from the held-out audit set.** Those 206 conversations are the only
   contamination-free measuring stick for the C2 lineage; training on them destroys it. Exclude by
   `user_turn_fingerprint` (`data/heldout_clean_set.py`), the same key
   `build_heldout_clean_set.py` uses.

**Do not inject edited completions into GRPO groups.** GRPO weights samples by logprobs under the
current policy; hand-edited completions are off-policy and would bias the gradient. If pairs are the
tool, use a preference objective built for them.

---

## 8. Reproducing

```bash
# Per-turn diagnostic (50 steps) — optimizer gate, saturated reward
./scripts/run_phase2_grpo.sh --skip-filter \
    --grpo-config configs/training/grpo_cat_a_c2_diagnostic.yaml \
    --sft-checkpoint checkpoints/sft_cat_a_c2/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it/checkpoint-1767

# Trajectory mode (10 steps) @ T=0.8, then the exploration probe @ T=1.4
./scripts/run_phase2_grpo.sh --skip-filter \
    --grpo-config configs/training/grpo_cat_a_c2_trajectory.yaml \
    --sft-checkpoint checkpoints/sft_cat_a_c2/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it/checkpoint-1767
./scripts/run_phase2_grpo.sh --skip-filter \
    --grpo-config configs/training/grpo_cat_a_c2_trajectory_temp.yaml \
    --sft-checkpoint checkpoints/sft_cat_a_c2/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it/checkpoint-1767
```

Read `reward`, `reward_std`, `frac_reward_zero_std` and
`train/unique_completions_per_group` from the step logs. `uniq == N` with `reward_std == 0` is the
signature of the resolution ceiling: the policy varied and the reward could not tell.

All runs used `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`. Every checkpoint directory is distinct
per config (`output_dir`), because `grpo.py` auto-resumes from the highest checkpoint it finds and a
shared directory silently continues another run's trajectory (R13).

input.content:
# What the last five commits did

The last five commits close out one investigation and start a new one.

Commit `35bff48` ran a probe. It raised the GRPO temperature from 0.8 to 1.4.
The goal was to test if higher temperature could restore reward variance.

Commit `51624ee` recorded the result. The result is negative. GRPO cannot
learn on this task. The reward reaches the value 1.0 on 81% of real
completions. Tied rewards give GRPO a zero gradient. Three fixes were tried.
None of them fixed the problem. The doc recommends preference learning
instead: DPO or ORPO on chosen/rejected pairs.

Commit `165f2cc` built the first pair set. It holds 29,256 training pairs and
3,450 validation pairs. Each pair has a gold turn and a corrupted turn. The
corruption mirrors a real failure of the current checkpoint (C2).

Commit `de950ec` added a second source of negatives. It mines negatives from
the checkpoint's own wrong generations, not from synthetic corruption. This
matters because R18 warns that synthetic-only negatives teach the model to
reject the corruption pattern, not to do the task correctly.

Commit `dc84adb` recorded the first mining run. It scored 399 checkpoint
generations. Only 51 of them were wrong (12.8%). This is lower than the
38.0% error rate seen on the held-out audit. The commit does not yet explain
why.

# What should we do next

**1. Write the DPO or ORPO trainer.**
This is the missing piece. The pair data exists. No trainer exists yet.
Search of the repo confirms there is no `training/dpo.py` and no
`configs/training/dpo_cat_a.yaml`. Follow the pattern of `training/grpo.py`:
one entry point, one config file, one set of unit tests with a mocked model.

**2. Merge the two negative sources into one training set.**
Combine the synthetic pairs from `165f2cc` and the mined pairs from
`de950ec`. Tag each pair with its `source` field, `synthetic` or `model`, so
you can measure the effect of each source later.

**3. Investigate the low mining yield.**
51 of 399 is far below the predicted 30%. Two theories are listed in the
commit message but neither is tested. Check them before you mine more
negatives, or you may waste GPU time on the wrong sample.

**4. Fix the known `run_phase2_grpo.sh` bug (R17).**
The GRPO launch script writes its patched config to a fixed path. A second
run can silently overwrite the first run's config. `run_phase2_sft.sh` had
the same bug and was already fixed. Port the same fix.

**5. Run the DPO or ORPO training job.**
Do this only after steps 1 through 3 are done.

# What you can do without a GPU

Everything in this project splits cleanly into two kinds of work: code and
data on one side, model runs on the other. Here is the without-GPU list.

- Write `training/dpo.py` and its config file.
- Write unit tests for the new trainer, with a mocked model (see
  `.claude/rules/08-testing.md`, "GRPO smoke: 10 steps with mock reward" for
  the pattern).
- Merge and tag the two preference-pair sources.
- Read the mining script and the audit numbers to test the two yield
  theories. This is data analysis, not a GPU job.
- Fix the `run_phase2_grpo.sh` config-path bug and add a regression test,
  matching `tests/unit/test_sft_output_dir.py`.
- Run `dvc pull` to fetch the tracked preference-pair data, then inspect it.
- Update `CLAUDE.md` and the docs once each step above is done.

# What still needs a GPU

- Mining more negatives from the checkpoint (`scripts/mine_model_negatives.py`).
- Running the DPO or ORPO training job itself.
- Any held-out eval that scores real model generations.

# Model Routing: Fable → Opus/Sonnet Handover

Use the most capable model where judgment quality compounds (specs, research, plans), and cheaper/faster models where the work is well-specified. A great spec executed by Sonnet beats a mediocre spec executed by Fable.

## Model tiers

| Model | Model string | Use for | Relative cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fable 5 | `claude-fable-5` | Spec drafting, deep research, planning, architecture trade-offs, ambiguous/novel problems | Highest — **always ask user first** |
| Opus 4.8 | `claude-opus-4-8` | Hard implementation: multi-file refactors, concurrency, performance-critical code, subtle debugging | High |
| Sonnet 5 | `claude-sonnet-5` | Routine implementation: CRUD, UI from a spec, tests, scripts, config, docs | Moderate |

## Routing decision

Classify the task **before** doing any work:

**Route to Fable (thinking work) when the task is:**
- Drafting a technical spec, PRD, or design doc from vague requirements
- Research requiring synthesis across many sources or deep domain reasoning
- System/architecture planning with non-obvious trade-offs (e.g., serving-engine selection, capacity modeling)
- Decomposing an ambiguous goal into an implementation plan
- Reviewing/critiquing a plan where a missed flaw is expensive

**Route to Opus (hard implementation) when ≥2 of these hold:**
- Touches >5 files or crosses module/service boundaries
- Involves concurrency, distributed state, or performance constraints
- Requires debugging with non-obvious root cause
- Correctness failures are costly (data loss, prod outage, security)
- The spec leaves meaningful design decisions to the implementer

**Route to Sonnet (routine implementation) when:**
- The spec/plan is complete and unambiguous
- The task is pattern-following: boilerplate, tests, UI from wireframes, glue code, migrations from a template
- Failures are cheap to detect and retry (lint/tests catch them)

Default when uncertain between Opus and Sonnet: start with Sonnet, escalate to Opus on the second failed attempt at the same problem.

## Fable confirmation gate (mandatory)

Never invoke Fable silently. Before any Fable call:

1. State **what** the Fable task is (one sentence).
2. State **why** a lower tier is insufficient.
3. Ask: "Use Fable for this? (highest-cost tier)"
4. Proceed only on explicit yes. If declined, do the task with Opus and note the downgrade.

This applies per work item, not per session — a new spec or research question needs a fresh confirmation. Batching is fine: "Use Fable for these 3 planning items?" counts as one confirmation for all three.

## Execution mechanics

**In Claude Code:**
- Delegate to a specific model via subagent: `Task(..., model="claude-sonnet-5")` (or opus/fable string)
- Or headless: `claude -p "<task>" --model claude-opus-4-8`
- Or tell the user to run `/model` to switch the interactive session

**Via API:** use the model strings from the table in the `model` field.

**If model switching isn't available in the current environment:** do the routing analysis anyway, tell the user which model should handle each phase, and produce the handover document so they can paste it into a session with the right model.

## Handover protocol (Fable → implementer)

Fable's output is only as useful as its handover. Every Fable planning/spec task must end with a handover document containing:

```markdown
# Handover: <task name>
**Target model:** claude-opus-4-8 | claude-sonnet-5 (with one-line justification)

## Objective
What done looks like, in one paragraph. Include acceptance criteria.

## Context the implementer lacks
Repo layout, key files, domain constraints, decisions already made and WHY.
Assume zero shared memory — the implementer sees only this document.

## Plan
Ordered steps. For Sonnet targets: fully specified, no open design questions.
For Opus targets: mark decisions intentionally left open with [IMPLEMENTER DECIDES].

## Constraints & non-goals
What must not change, out-of-scope items, performance/compat requirements.

## Verification
Exact commands/tests to run to confirm success.
```

Rules:
- **Sonnet handovers must contain zero open design questions.** If a question remains, either resolve it in the plan or upgrade the target to Opus.
- Include concrete file paths, function names, and interface signatures — not "update the relevant module."
- If the plan exceeds ~1 day of implementation work, split into multiple handover docs, each independently verifiable.

## Multi-phase workflow example

User: "Build a rate limiter for our voicebot API."

1. Classify: ambiguous requirements + architecture trade-offs → Fable task.
2. Ask: "This needs algorithm selection (token bucket vs sliding window) and capacity modeling — use Fable for the design spec? (highest-cost tier)"
3. On yes → Fable produces spec + handover doc. Distributed-state coordination piece → target Opus. Config, metrics endpoint, and tests → target Sonnet (separate handover).
4. Delegate each handover to its target model; run verification commands from each doc before accepting.

## Anti-patterns

- Using Fable for work a complete spec already covers — waste.
- Handing Sonnet a plan with "figure out the best approach for X" — that's an Opus task or an incomplete plan.
- Escalating to Fable after one Sonnet failure — try Opus first; Fable is for thinking, not retry-firepower.
- Skipping the confirmation because the user approved Fable earlier in the session for a different item.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /workspaces/ai-agent-llms/.claude/skills/model-training-eval

# Model Training & Evaluation Skill

Design, debug, and reason about training pipelines for any trainable ML model — LLMs, vision, speech, RL, tabular, multimodal, time-series, and classical models — with the rigor of a senior ML practitioner.

This skill treats training as a system: data → optimization → evaluation → analysis. Most "model" problems are really data, optimization, or evaluation problems in disguise. The skill's job is to make that visible and fixable.

## Service Modes

| Mode | Trigger | Output |
|------|---------|--------|
| **Pipeline Design** | "design a training pipeline", "how should I train", "set up SFT/pretraining/RL", "training architecture" | End-to-end pipeline spec |
| **Debug** | "loss is NaN", "not converging", "exploding gradients", "model isn't learning", "training crashed" | Diagnostic walkthrough + fixes |
| **Dynamics Analysis** | "analyze loss curve", "is my training healthy", "interpret gradients", "explain the metrics" | Annotated analysis with signals |
| **Evaluation Design** | "how to evaluate", "design benchmarks", "eval protocol", "metrics for X" | Eval framework with splits, metrics, leakage controls |
| **Optimization** | "train faster", "reduce memory", "improve sample efficiency", "tune hyperparameters" | Concrete optimization plan |
| **Review** | "review my training code", "audit this pipeline", "is this setup correct" | Findings list with severity + fixes |

The modes overlap and can chain (e.g., a debug session often ends in an optimization or design change). Use the mode that fits the user's primary intent; pull in others as needed.

---

## Core Mental Model

Before any concrete work, anchor on this mental model — it shapes every downstream decision:

**A training run is a controlled experiment.** It has a hypothesis (this architecture + data + objective will produce this capability), an intervention (the training loop), and a measurement (evaluation). When the result is wrong, the cause lives in one of four places:

1. **Data** — Wrong distribution, leakage, label noise, tokenization mismatch, augmentation bug, split contamination
2. **Objective** — Wrong loss, mismatched labels, masked-out targets, reward misspecification, regularization too strong/weak
3. **Optimization** — LR too high/low, bad schedule, optimizer mismatch, numerical instability, distributed sync bug
4. **Evaluation** — Test leakage, wrong metric, prompt/format mismatch, judge bias, insufficient samples

**Always diagnose in this order.** Data first, evaluation last. The reason: data bugs masquerade as everything else, and evaluation bugs make you chase phantoms.

A second mental model worth holding: **the model is the easiest thing to change and almost never the actual problem.** Treat "swap the model" as a last resort, not a first move.

---

## Universal Training Workflow

Use this as the scaffold for Pipeline Design mode and as the diagnostic frame for Debug/Analysis modes.

```
1. Frame the problem → 2. Build the data pipeline → 3. Establish baselines → 4. Train with instrumentation → 5. Evaluate rigorously → 6. Iterate
```

### Step 1: Frame the Problem

Capture the following before writing any code. If the user hasn't specified one of these, ask — guessing leads to wasted compute.

- **Task type**: supervised / self-supervised / RL / contrastive / generative / etc.
- **Inputs and outputs**: shapes, dtypes, modalities, max sequence length, label space
- **Success metric**: what *primary* metric decides if this worked, plus 1-3 guardrails
- **Compute envelope**: GPUs/TPUs available, memory per device, time budget, training framework
- **Constraints**: latency at inference, model size limit, deployment target, regulatory/PII constraints
- **What "good" looks like**: a concrete number, behavior, or comparison ("beat the current production model on metric X by Y%")

Output a one-page **Problem Card** capturing the above. This is the contract for the rest of the work.

### Step 2: Build the Data Pipeline

Data quality dominates model quality. Build the data pipeline before the model, not after.

**Data pipeline checklist:**

- [ ] Source data inventory: where it comes from, license, freshness, size, schema
- [ ] Split strategy: random / stratified / time-based / group-based — chosen for the *deployment* distribution
- [ ] Leakage audit: no future info in past splits, no identity leakage across train/test, no label leakage in features
- [ ] Preprocessing pipeline: deterministic, versioned, separately runnable
- [ ] Augmentation strategy: applied only to train, not val/test; consistent with deployment-time inputs
- [ ] Quality checks: distribution stats, null/inf checks, label distribution, duplicate detection
- [ ] Loader: streaming if data > RAM, shuffled, packed (for sequence models), correctly batched
- [ ] Sample inspection: literally look at 20 random examples — every time, every dataset

See `references/pipeline-design.md` for domain-specific data pipeline patterns (LLM packing, CV augmentation, RL replay buffers, tabular CV, etc.).

### Step 3: Establish Baselines

Never start with a fancy model. Establish a ladder of baselines so you can attribute later improvements:

1. **Trivial baseline**: predict majority class / mean / zero / random — to confirm the metric is sane
2. **Simple baseline**: a shallow model or a tiny version of the target architecture
3. **Strong baseline**: published SOTA or current production model, run on the same eval

**Overfit a tiny batch first** (Karpathy's recipe). Take 2-32 samples, turn off regularization, and verify loss → near-zero. If a model cannot memorize a handful of examples, it cannot learn the real task — and the bug is almost certainly in your code, not your hyperparameters.

### Step 4: Train with Instrumentation

Instrument every run so that *if it fails, you can tell why without rerunning*. The cost of logging is trivial; the cost of a re-run on H100s is not.

**Always log:**

- Loss (per batch and smoothed) — and any auxiliary losses separately
- Gradient norm (global and per-parameter-group)
- Weight norm and weight update ratio (||Δw|| / ||w||) — target ~1e-3 for healthy SGD
- Learning rate (especially across schedule transitions)
- Throughput (samples/sec, tokens/sec) and GPU utilization
- Memory (peak per device)
- Validation metrics at a meaningful cadence

**Always save:**

- Run config (every hyperparameter, every flag, frozen as JSON/YAML)
- Code state (commit hash + diff if dirty)
- Environment (framework versions, CUDA, GPU type, seed)
- Periodic checkpoints (not just the last one)

See `references/training-dynamics.md` for how to interpret these signals.

### Step 5: Evaluate Rigorously

Evaluation is what makes the run *mean* something. Common eval failures: contamination, prompt-format mismatch, single-seed reporting, metric-on-wrong-distribution, judge bias.

**Eval design checklist:**

- [ ] Held-out test set never seen during training (incl. via dataset reuse)
- [ ] Eval distribution matches deployment distribution (or known mismatch is documented)
- [ ] Primary metric + guardrails reported together
- [ ] Multiple seeds where stochasticity matters (mean ± std)
- [ ] Per-stratum breakdowns (per-class, per-length, per-subpopulation)
- [ ] Statistical significance vs. baseline (paired bootstrap or t-test)
- [ ] Failure-mode analysis: look at the worst N predictions

See `references/evaluation-frameworks.md` for domain-specific eval protocols.

### Step 6: Iterate

Iterate as a sequence of controlled changes, one variable at a time, each tracked.

**Iteration template per change:**

- Hypothesis (what you expect to happen and why)
- Change (single variable, ideally)
- Result (delta on primary + guardrails)
- Decision (keep / revert / extend)
- Notes (anything surprising — these are gold)

Resist the urge to change three things at once. When you must, plan an ablation to attribute the win/loss.

---

## Debugging Methodology

When a training run misbehaves, use the **diagnostic ladder**. Climb in order — each rung is cheaper to check than the one above.

### The Diagnostic Ladder

| Rung | Check | Why it goes here |
|------|-------|------------------|
| 1 | **Did anything change recently?** Code, data, env, hardware? | Most regressions have an obvious culprit if you look |
| 2 | **Sanity check the data.** Print 10 batches. Inputs make sense? Labels match? Shapes/dtypes/devices right? Mask correct? | 50%+ of "training bugs" are data bugs |
| 3 | **Overfit a tiny batch.** 4-32 samples, no regularization. Does loss → 0? | Isolates code bugs from training/data bugs |
| 4 | **Check the loss numerics.** NaN / Inf / negative-when-shouldn't-be / suspiciously constant? | Cheap to inspect, tells you a lot |
| 5 | **Check gradient flow.** Per-layer grad norms — any zero or exploding? | Reveals dead layers, init issues, exploding paths |
| 6 | **Check optimizer state.** LR actually as configured? Schedule firing? Optimizer betas reasonable? | Schedule bugs are silent and common |
| 7 | **Check distributed sync.** Same loss across ranks? Gradients all-reduced? Effective batch right? | Multi-GPU bugs are invisible until they aren't |
| 8 | **Check eval.** Is the metric well-defined? Eval on train — does it match training loss? | Eval bugs can fake regressions |
| 9 | **Now consider model/hyperparameter changes.** | Last, not first |

See `references/debugging-playbook.md` for the full failure-mode catalog organized by symptom (NaN, plateau, train-val gap, OOM, slow throughput, distributed deadlock, reproducibility break, etc.).

### When You Genuinely Don't Know

If the ladder doesn't reveal the cause:

1. **Bisect the change set.** Find the last known-good commit; binary-search to the regression.
2. **Reduce to a minimal repro.** Smallest model, smallest batch, single GPU, smallest dataset that still shows the bug.
3. **Diff against a working baseline.** A canonical example (HF, official repo) running on your environment. Differences are the search space.
4. **Print everything.** When in doubt, log more. Don't trust your assumptions about what the values are.

---

## Training Dynamics Quick Reference

Use this table when reading a loss curve or training log. For deeper interpretation, see `references/training-dynamics.md`.

| Signal | Healthy | Warning | Common Cause |
|--------|---------|---------|--------------|
| Train loss | Decreasing, then plateaus | NaN, increasing, flat-from-start | LR too high, bad init, dead loss, frozen layer |
| Val loss | Tracks train, eventually plateaus or rises slightly | Diverges early from train | Overfitting, data leak inverse, distribution shift |
| Grad norm | Stable order of magnitude, decreasing | Spikes, NaN, → 0 across all layers | Outlier batch, exploding/vanishing gradients |
| Per-layer grads | All non-zero | Some zero, some huge | Dead layer, no skip connection, bad init |
| ||Δw|| / ||w|| | ~1e-3 | <1e-5 or >1e-2 | LR mis-set for this architecture |
| Activation stats | Stable mean ~0, std ~1 (post-norm) | Drifting, saturating | Norm layer misuse, init mismatch |
| Throughput | Constant | Degrading | Memory fragmentation, data loader stall, thermal |
| GPU util | >85% during compute phase | <50% sustained | Data loader bottleneck, small batch, sync overhead |
| LR schedule | Matches plan | Doesn't decay / spikes | Schedule misconfigured, step count off |

---

## Cross-Domain Principles

These hold across LLMs, CV, RL, tabular, and beyond. They earn their place in the SKILL.md (not a reference) because they prevent the most expensive mistakes.

1. **The deployment distribution is the only one that matters.** Train, validate, and evaluate on data that reflects it. If you can't, document the gap and design probes for it.

2. **Reproducibility is a feature, not a chore.** Pin seeds, framework versions, CUDA, data versions, code state. A run you can't reproduce is a run you can't debug.

3. **Compute spent on iteration speed pays itself back.** Faster eval, smaller dev set, better logging, quicker checkpoints — these compound across experiments.

4. **Most "the model is bad" findings are eval bugs.** Before declaring failure, eval the *previous* known-good model on the new eval to sanity-check.

5. **Make every experiment attributable.** One change at a time, tracked, with a written hypothesis. Heroic 12-change sprints destroy learning.

6. **Save the boring things.** Tokenizers, normalizers, label maps, vocabularies. These vanish silently and break things weeks later.

7. **Watch for silent failures.** Off-by-one masks, swapped channels, wrong device, padding included in loss, augmentation applied to val. These don't crash; they corrode.

8. **Cheap signals beat expensive signals.** Loss on a tiny eval every step beats a perfect eval every epoch. Calibrate the cost/info trade-off.

---

## Output Formats by Mode

### Pipeline Design Mode

```markdown
# Training Pipeline: [Task Name]

## 1. Problem Card
- Task type, inputs/outputs, success metric, compute envelope, constraints

## 2. Data Pipeline
- Sources, splits (with rationale), preprocessing, augmentation, quality checks, loader spec

## 3. Model & Objective
- Architecture choice + rationale, loss function, regularization, init scheme

## 4. Optimization
- Optimizer + hyperparameters, LR schedule, batch size, gradient accumulation, precision

## 5. Distributed / Hardware
- Parallelism strategy (DP/DDP/FSDP/TP/PP), memory budget, checkpointing

## 6. Instrumentation
- Logged metrics, checkpoint cadence, eval cadence, tracking backend

## 7. Evaluation Protocol
- Primary metric, guardrails, splits, statistical methodology

## 8. Risk Register
- Top 3-5 things most likely to go wrong + how we'll detect them

## 9. Iteration Plan
- Baselines → ablations → optimizations, in order
```

### Debug Mode

```markdown
# Debug Report: [Symptom]

## Symptom
[Concise description with evidence — log snippet, metric value, error]

## Diagnostic Walk
- Rung 1: [check] → [result]
- Rung 2: [check] → [result]
- ...

## Root Cause
[The actual cause, with evidence]

## Fix
[Minimal change to resolve. Code or config diff.]

## Prevention
[Logging / assertion / test that would have caught this earlier]
```

### Dynamics Analysis Mode

```markdown
# Training Dynamics Analysis

## Run Summary
[Config, duration, hardware, primary metrics]

## Signal-by-Signal Read
- Loss: [healthy / warning + evidence]
- Gradients: [...]
- Weights & updates: [...]
- Throughput: [...]
- Eval: [...]

## Interpretation
[What the combined signals say about training health]

## Recommendations
[Concrete next steps, ranked by expected impact]
```

### Evaluation Design Mode

```markdown
# Evaluation Framework: [Task]

## Goal
[What this eval is trying to measure and decide]

## Splits
- Train/val/test definition + rationale for split type
- Contamination controls

## Metrics
- Primary: [metric] — why
- Guardrails: [list] — why
- Per-stratum breakdowns: [list]

## Methodology
- Sample size + power justification
- Seeds, runs, aggregation
- Statistical comparison method

## Known Limitations
[Eval gaps and how to mitigate]
```

### Optimization Mode

```markdown
# Optimization Plan

## Current State
[Throughput, memory, time-to-target, primary metric]

## Bottleneck Analysis
[Where time/memory is actually going — profiler evidence]

## Proposed Changes (ordered by impact / cost)
1. [Change] → expected gain → effort → risk
2. ...

## Validation Plan
[How to verify each change doesn't regress quality]
```

### Review Mode

```markdown
# Training Pipeline Review

## Summary
[1-2 sentence verdict]

## Findings
| ID | Severity | Area | Finding | Suggested Fix |
|----|----------|------|---------|---------------|
| 1 | Critical | Data | ... | ... |

## Strengths
[What's working well]

## Recommendations Prioritized
[Top 3-5 actions]
```

---

## When to Read Which Reference

- **`references/pipeline-design.md`** — designing or reviewing a training pipeline for a specific domain (LLM SFT, CV detection, RL policy gradient, tabular GBM, etc.)
- **`references/debugging-playbook.md`** — diagnosing a specific symptom (NaN, plateau, OOM, distributed failure, reproducibility break, etc.)
- **`references/training-dynamics.md`** — interpreting loss curves, gradient stats, calibration, scaling behavior
- **`references/evaluation-frameworks.md`** — designing rigorous evals for a specific domain, including contamination controls and statistical methodology
- **`references/domain-recipes.md`** — quick recipes and known-good configs by domain (LLM, CV, RL, speech, tabular, multimodal, time-series)

Read the relevant reference whenever the user's question is more specific than this SKILL.md covers. The references are deeper and more concrete; this file is the navigation layer.

---

## Quality Gates

Before delivering, check:

- [ ] Mode-appropriate output format used
- [ ] Concrete recommendations, not generic advice
- [ ] Trade-offs and risks named, not glossed
- [ ] Numbers, ranges, or thresholds given where applicable (not just "tune the LR")
- [ ] Domain-specific reference consulted when domain is non-trivial
- [ ] Diagnostic order followed (data → objective → optimization → evaluation)
- [ ] Reproducibility considered (seeds, versions, config capture)
- [ ] Eval distribution alignment with deployment considered

"""Internal shared utilities for training modules.

Extracted here to avoid importing private functions across sibling modules.
All heavy imports (torch, transformers) are deferred to function bodies.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from llm_workflow_agents.config.schema import TrainingModelConfig


def normalize_chat_template_ids(out: Any) -> list[int]:
    """Normalize ``apply_chat_template(tokenize=True)`` output to ``list[int]``.

    transformers 5.x returns a ``BatchEncoding`` where 4.x returned a plain
    list, and processors may return a batched tensor. This has broken two call
    sites in two different ways — silently in
    ``sft.py::render_response_only_sample`` (``list(mapping)`` yields the KEYS,
    so samples rendered as 2 tokens with 0 unmasked labels and training signal
    vanished without a crash; bac1d98) and loudly in
    ``trajectory_rollout.py::_derive_turn_end_id`` (``int(ids[-1])`` raising on
    a ``tokenizers.Encoding``, which disabled trajectory rollouts entirely).

    The second happened because the first was fixed in place instead of shared.
    Both now call this.

    Order is load-bearing: unwrap the mapping **before** any list coercion,
    because ``list(BatchEncoding)`` succeeds and returns key names rather than
    raising. A mapping without ``input_ids`` raises ``KeyError`` — failing
    loudly beats silently returning something list-shaped and wrong.
    """
    if isinstance(out, Mapping):
        out = out["input_ids"]
    if hasattr(out, "tolist"):
        out = out.tolist()
    if len(out) and isinstance(out[0], (list, tuple)):
        out = out[0]
    return [int(x) for x in out]


def _build_training_arguments(config: TrainingModelConfig, output_dir: Path) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build HuggingFace TrainingArguments kwargs from config."""
    micro_batch_size = config.training.effective_batch_size // config.training.gradient_accumulation_steps

    args_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {
        "output_dir": str(output_dir),
        "per_device_train_batch_size": micro_batch_size,
        "gradient_accumulation_steps": config.training.gradient_accumulation_steps,
        "learning_rate": config.training.learning_rate,
        "lr_scheduler_type": config.training.lr_scheduler,
        "warmup_ratio": config.training.warmup_ratio,
        "num_train_epochs": config.training.num_epochs,
        "max_seq_length": config.training.max_seq_length,
        "logging_steps": 10,
        "save_strategy": config.training.save_strategy,
        "save_steps": config.training.save_steps,
        "eval_strategy": "steps",
        "eval_steps": config.training.eval_steps,
        "load_best_model_at_end": True,
        "metric_for_best_model": config.training.metric_for_best_model,
        "greater_is_better": False,
        "report_to": "wandb",
        "remove_unused_columns": False,
        "gradient_checkpointing": config.training.gradient_checkpointing,
    }

    # Precision
    if config.training.mixed_precision == "bf16":
        args_kwargs["bf16"] = True
    elif config.training.mixed_precision == "fp16":
        args_kwargs["fp16"] = True

    # Gradient checkpointing kwargs
    if config.training.gradient_checkpointing:
        args_kwargs["gradient_checkpointing_kwargs"] = {"use_reentrant": False}

    return args_kwargs

4	(data paths, chat templates) is driven by config YAML.

23	_LOSS_MASK_RESPONSE_ONLY = "response_only"

27	def _sft_length_kwargs(training_cfg: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
28	    """Sequence-length kwargs for ``SFTConfig``, keyed to the installed TRL.
29	
30	    Pre-tokenizing to ``max_seq_length`` in ``_render_chat`` is NOT sufficient.
31	    TRL builds ``DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(max_length=args.max_length,
32	    truncation_mode=args.truncation_mode)`` and re-truncates every batch, and
33	    ``SFTConfig.max_length`` defaults to **1024**. With the default
34	    ``truncation_mode='keep_start'`` that keeps the first 1024 tokens of each
35	    sample.
36	
37	    For Task A the enriched system prompt alone is a median 3,016 tokens, so
38	    that window is pure system prompt:
39	
40	    - under ``all_tokens`` the run trains on a near-identical prefix across all
41	      examples — cheap loss, high token accuracy, little transferable skill;
42	    - under ``response_only`` every retained token is masked to -100, there are
43	      no valid targets, and loss/grad/accuracy are exactly 0.
44	
45	    ``max_seq_length`` was a ``SFTConfig`` kwarg through TRL 0.22 and was
46	    renamed to ``max_length`` in 0.23+, so pass whichever the installed version
47	    accepts rather than assuming either.
48	    """
49	    from trl import SFTConfig
50	
51	    max_seq = training_cfg.get("max_seq_length", 8192)
52	    params = inspect.signature(SFTConfig).parameters
53	    kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {}
54	    if "max_length" in params:
55	        kwargs["max_length"] = max_seq
56	    if "max_seq_length" in params:  # TRL <= 0.22
57	        kwargs["max_seq_length"] = max_seq
58	    return kwargs

61	def _sft_eval_batch_size(
62	    training_cfg: dict[str, Any], per_device_train_bs: int
63	) -> int:
64	    """Per-device eval batch size. TRL defaults this to 8; we default to the
65	    train batch size.
66	
67	    The eval forward materializes fp32 logits of shape
68	    ``(batch, seq, vocab)``. Gemma-4's vocab is 262,144, so at 8192 tokens a
69	    batch of 8 needs ``8 * 8192 * 262144 * 4B`` ~= 68 GiB in a single
70	    allocation — an instant OOM on an 80GB card, and it would not surface
71	    until the first eval at save_steps, hours into a run.
72	
73	    This never bit historically only because the collator was silently
74	    truncating every sample to 1024 tokens (see R16 / _sft_length_kwargs),
75	    making the same tensor 8x smaller.
76	    """
77	    return int(training_cfg.get("per_device_eval_batch_size", per_device_train_bs))

80	def render_response_only_sample(
81	    messages: list[dict[str, str]],
82	    tokenizer: Any,
83	    max_seq_length: int,
84	) -> dict[str, list[int]]:
85	    """Tokenize one conversation, masking non-assistant spans to -100.
86	
87	    Walks `messages` incrementally: for each turn, tokenizes
88	    `apply_chat_template(prefix)` and `apply_chat_template(prefix + turn)` and
89	    takes the delta. Tokens from non-assistant turns get label -100; assistant
90	    tokens carry through unmasked. Truncates from the left so the final
91	    assistant turn always survives.
92	
93	    Chat-template-agnostic — relies only on `apply_chat_template`'s
94	    deterministic prefix-extension behavior. Used by Recipe B (response_only)
95	    in docs/fine_tuning_recipes.md.
96	
97	    Returns {"input_ids", "attention_mask", "labels"} for a single sample.
98	    """
99	    from llm_workflow_agents.training._utils import normalize_chat_template_ids
100	
101	    ids: list[int] = []
102	    labels: list[int] = []
103	
104	    def _encode(msgs: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[int]:
105	        if not msgs:
106	            return []
107	        # Normalization lives in _utils so sft.py and trajectory_rollout.py
108	        # share one implementation. Keeping a private copy here is what let
109	        # transformers 5.x break the rollout path months after bac1d98 fixed
110	        # the identical issue in this function. See the helper's docstring for
111	        # why the mapping must be unwrapped before any list coercion.
112	        return normalize_chat_template_ids(
113	            tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
114	                msgs, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=False
115	            )
116	        )
117	
118	    prev_encoded: list[int] = []
119	    for i, msg in enumerate(messages):
120	        extended = _encode(messages[: i + 1])
121	        # Guard against tokenizers that don't deterministically extend
122	        # (rare; e.g. some templates re-render BOS). Fall back to encoding
123	        # this turn alone if the prefix doesn't match the head of `extended`.
124	        if (
125	            len(extended) >= len(prev_encoded)
126	            and extended[: len(prev_encoded)] == prev_encoded
127	        ):
128	            new = extended[len(prev_encoded) :]
129	        else:
130	            new = _encode([msg])
131	            extended = prev_encoded + new
132	        ids.extend(new)
133	        if msg.get("role") == "assistant":
134	            labels.extend(new)
135	        else:
136	            labels.extend([-100] * len(new))
137	        prev_encoded = extended
138	
139	    # Left-truncate to preserve the final assistant turn.
140	    if len(ids) > max_seq_length:
141	        cut = len(ids) - max_seq_length
142	        ids = ids[cut:]
143	        labels = labels[cut:]
144	
145	    return {
146	        "input_ids": ids,
147	        "attention_mask": [1] * len(ids),
148	        "labels": labels,
149	    }
150	
151	
152	#: Bump to invalidate every cached render at once, e.g. when the cache
153	#: format itself changes rather than the rendering code.
154	_RENDER_CACHE_VERSION = 1
155	
156	_RENDER_CACHE_DEFAULT_DIR = Path(".cache/sft_render")
157	
158	_FALSEY = {"0", "false", "no", "off"}
159	
160	
161	def _render_code_version() -> str:
162	    """Digest of the code that decides what a rendered sample looks like.
163	
164	    Two sources beyond the corpus file change the rendered bytes:
165	
166	    - ``render_response_only_sample`` — the per-turn tokenize/mask walk;
167	    - ``data/system_prompt.py`` — ``_load_split`` rebuilds ``messages[0]`` with
168	      ``build_enriched_system_prompt(force_rebuild=True)``, so a prompt edit
169	      re-renders every sample with the corpus byte-identical.
170	
171	    Hashing them keeps a stale cache from silently outliving the code that
172	    produced it. Editing the prompt builder invalidates every entry, which is
173	    the intended trade: a spurious re-render costs minutes, a wrong one costs
174	    a training run.
175	    """
176	    import hashlib
177	    import inspect
178	
179	    from llm_workflow_agents.data import system_prompt as _system_prompt
180	
181	    h = hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=16)
182	    h.update(str(_RENDER_CACHE_VERSION).encode())
183	    h.update(inspect.getsource(render_response_only_sample).encode())
184	    h.update(Path(_system_prompt.__file__).read_bytes())
185	    return h.hexdigest()
186	
187	
188	def _tokenizer_identity(tokenizer: Any) -> str:
189	    """Identity string for the tokenizer/processor driving the render.
190	
191	    Gemma-4's ``FastLanguageModel`` hands back a multimodal Processor whose
192	    chat template and vocabulary live on a nested ``.tokenizer``, so read both
193	    levels and tolerate either being absent.
194	    """
195	    parts: list[str] = []
196	    for obj in (tokenizer, getattr(tokenizer, "tokenizer", None)):
197	        if obj is None:
198	            continue
199	        parts.append(str(getattr(obj, "name_or_path", "")))
200	        parts.append(str(getattr(obj, "chat_template", "") or ""))
201	        parts.append(str(getattr(obj, "vocab_size", "")))
202	    return "\x00".join(parts)

205	def _render_cache_fingerprint(
206	    *,
207	    split_path: Path,
208	    loss_mask: str,
209	    max_seq_length: int,
210	    tokenizer: Any,
211	) -> str:
212	    """Hex key over everything that changes a split's rendered output.
213	
214	    Covers the split's full contents (not mtime/size — a regenerated corpus can
215	    land at the same size), the recipe, the tokenizer, and the render code.
216	    """
217	    import hashlib
218	
219	    h = hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=16)
220	
221	    def _field(value: Any) -> None:
222	        h.update(str(value).encode())
223	        h.update(b"\x00")
224	
225	    _field(_render_code_version())
226	    _field(loss_mask)
227	    _field(max_seq_length)
228	    _field(_tokenizer_identity(tokenizer))
229	    _field(Path(split_path).name)
230	
231	    with open(split_path, "rb") as fh:
232	        for chunk in iter(lambda: fh.read(4 << 20), b""):
233	            h.update(chunk)
234	
235	    return h.hexdigest()

238	def _render_cache_dir(data_cfg: dict[str, Any]) -> Path | None:
239	    """Where rendered splits are cached, or ``None`` when caching is off.
240	
241	    On by default. ``data.render_cache: false`` or ``SFT_RENDER_CACHE=0``
242	    disables it; ``SFT_RENDER_CACHE_DIR`` relocates it.
243	    """
244	    if os.environ.get("SFT_RENDER_CACHE", "1").strip().lower() in _FALSEY:
245	        return None
246	    if not data_cfg.get("render_cache", True):
247	        return None
248	    override = os.environ.get("SFT_RENDER_CACHE_DIR")
249	    return Path(override) if override else _RENDER_CACHE_DEFAULT_DIR

252	def _render_split_cached(
253	    *,
254	    name: str,
255	    fingerprint: str,
256	    cache_dir: Path | None,
257	    build: Any,
258	) -> Any:
259	    """Return the rendered split, reusing a cached copy when the key matches.
260	
261	    ``response_only`` re-tokenizes every conversation prefix once per turn, so
262	    rendering Task A costs tens of minutes and is paid again on every resume.
263	
264	    Writes go to a staging directory and are renamed into place, so a run
265	    killed mid-save leaves no entry that a later resume would read as complete.
266	    A cache that cannot be read or written is a warning, never a failure —
267	    training falls back to rendering.
268	    """
269	    if cache_dir is None:
270	        return build()
271	
272	    import shutil
273	
274	    from datasets import load_from_disk
275	
276	    entry = Path(cache_dir) / f"{name}-{fingerprint}"
277	    if entry.exists():
278	        try:
279	            cached = load_from_disk(str(entry))
280	            logger.info(
281	                "sft_render_cache_hit", split=name, path=str(entry), rows=len(cached)
282	            )
283	            return cached
284	        except Exception as exc:  # cache is advisory — never fail a run on it
285	            logger.warning(
286	                "sft_render_cache_unreadable",
287	                split=name,
288	                path=str(entry),
289	                error=str(exc),
290	            )
291	
292	    rendered = build()
293	    staging = Path(cache_dir) / f".{name}-{fingerprint}.tmp-{os.getpid()}"
294	    try:
295	        Path(cache_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
296	        shutil.rmtree(staging, ignore_errors=True)
297	        rendered.save_to_disk(str(staging))
298	        shutil.rmtree(entry, ignore_errors=True)
299	        staging.rename(entry)
300	        logger.info(
301	            "sft_render_cache_store",
302	            split=name,
303	            path=str(entry),
304	            rows=len(rendered),
305	        )
306	    except Exception as exc:  # cache is advisory — never fail a run on it
307	        shutil.rmtree(staging, ignore_errors=True)
308	        logger.warning(
309	            "sft_render_cache_store_failed", split=name, path=str(entry), error=str(exc)
310	        )
311	    return rendered

314	def _prepare_split(
315	    *,
316	    name: str,
317	    data_source: Path | str,
318	    loss_mask: str,
319	    max_seq_length: int,
320	    tokenizer: Any,
321	    cache_dir: Path | None,
322	    load_split: Any,
323	    render_fn: Any,
324	) -> Any:
325	    """Load and render one split, serving a cached render when the key matches.
326	
327	    The fingerprint comes from the JSONL on disk, not from the loaded rows, so
328	    a hit skips the raw load and the system-prompt rebuild as well as the
329	    tokenize pass.
330	    """
331	    path = Path(data_source) / f"{name}.jsonl"
332	    if not path.exists():
333	        raise FileNotFoundError(f"SFT split missing: {path}")
334	
335	    fingerprint = _render_cache_fingerprint(
336	        split_path=path,
337	        loss_mask=loss_mask,
338	        max_seq_length=max_seq_length,
339	        tokenizer=tokenizer,
340	    )
341	
342	    def _build() -> Any:
343	        return load_split(name).map(
344	            render_fn, batched=True, remove_columns=["messages"]
345	        )
346	
347	    return _render_split_cached(
348	        name=name, fingerprint=fingerprint, cache_dir=cache_dir, build=_build
349	    )

380	def _resolve_output_dir(
381	    config: dict[str, Any], config_path: Path, model_name: str
382	) -> Path:
383	    """Resolve the checkpoint output directory for a run.
384	
385	    Precedence:
386	      1. Explicit ``output_dir`` in the config — the only way to give a run a
387	         distinct directory (e.g. one per factorial cell).
388	      2. The config filename stem, with any trailing run stamp removed.
389	
390	    The stamp strip matters: R13 made the patched config run-specific
391	    (``sft_cat_a_20260722T051246Z.yaml``), and deriving the output directory
392	    straight from that stem silently moved checkpoints to a per-run path that
393	    the DVC stage does not track, leaving the declared output weightless.
394	    Provenance belongs in the config filename; the checkpoint path must stay
395	    stable unless asked to change.

432	def _patch_gemma4_rope_stride(model: Any) -> int:
433	    """Force `inv_freq_expanded` contiguous in Gemma-4 RoPE — instance-level.
434	
435	    Why instance-level: Unsloth pre-generates a copy of the Gemma-4 module
436	    in `unsloth_compiled_cache/unsloth_compiled_module_gemma4.py` and
437	    routes calls through *that* module's own `patched_forward`, bypassing
438	    any class-level monkey-patch on transformers' `Gemma4TextRotaryEmbedding`.
439	    Patching the bound `forward` on each loaded module instance catches
440	    both code paths.
441	
442	    Root cause: the original forward builds `inv_freq_expanded` via
443	    `.expand(B, -1, 1)`, which is a stride-0 view on the batch dim.
444	    cuBLAS in CUDA 13 rejects batched sgemm with 0-stride batch
445	    (CUBLAS_STATUS_INVALID_VALUE); CUDA 12 was more permissive.
446	    `.contiguous()` materializes a real tensor before the matmul.
447	
448	    Returns the number of modules patched.
449	    """
450	    import torch
451	    from types import MethodType
452	
453	    try:
454	        from transformers.modeling_rope_utils import dynamic_rope_update
455	    except ImportError:
456	        def dynamic_rope_update(fn):  # type: ignore[no-redef]
457	            return fn
458	
459	    @torch.no_grad()
460	    @dynamic_rope_update
461	    def patched_forward(self, x, position_ids, layer_type=None):
462	        inv_freq = getattr(self, f"{layer_type}_inv_freq")
463	        attention_scaling = getattr(self, f"{layer_type}_attention_scaling")
464	
465	        # Build (B, N) and (B, S) tensors and use broadcast multiply,
466	        # mathematically identical to upstream's bmm of shape
467	        # (B, N, 1) @ (B, 1, S) since K=1 makes the sum trivial. This
468	        # avoids cuBLAS sgemm entirely — torch 2.10 + CUDA 13 cuBLAS
469	        # rejects K=1 batched sgemm with CUBLAS_STATUS_INVALID_VALUE.
470	        inv_freq_b = inv_freq[None, :].float().expand(position_ids.shape[0], -1).to(x.device)
471	        pos_f = position_ids.float()
472	
473	        device_type = (
474	            x.device.type
475	            if isinstance(x.device.type, str) and x.device.type != "mps"
476	            else "cpu"
477	        )
478	        with torch.amp.autocast(device_type=device_type, enabled=False):
479	            # (B, N, 1) * (B, 1, S) -> (B, N, S), then transpose to (B, S, N)
480	            freqs = (inv_freq_b.unsqueeze(-1) * pos_f.unsqueeze(1)).transpose(1, 2)
481	            emb = torch.cat((freqs, freqs), dim=-1)
482	            cos = emb.cos() * attention_scaling
483	            sin = emb.sin() * attention_scaling
484	
485	        return cos.to(dtype=x.dtype), sin.to(dtype=x.dtype)
486	
487	    patched = 0
488	    for module in model.modules():
489	        cls_name = type(module).__name__
490	        if cls_name not in {"Gemma4TextRotaryEmbedding", "Gemma4RotaryEmbedding"}:
491	            continue
492	        if getattr(module, "_unsloth_workflow_patched", False):
493	            continue
494	        module.forward = MethodType(patched_forward, module)
495	        module._unsloth_workflow_patched = True
496	        patched += 1
497	    if patched:
498	        logger.info("gemma4_rope_stride_patch_applied", instances=patched)
499	    else:
500	        logger.debug("gemma4_rope_stride_patch_skipped", reason="no Gemma-4 RoPE modules in model")
501	    return patched

504	def train_sft(
505	    config_path: Path,
506	    resume_from_checkpoint: bool | str | Path | None = None,
507	) -> SFTResult:
508	    """Run Unsloth SFT pipeline.
509	
510	    Pipeline:
511	      1. Load base model via FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained()
512	      2. Apply LoRA via FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model()
513	      3. Configure SFTTrainer with packing + per-model chat template
514	      4. Train for num_epochs, checkpoint every 500 steps
515	      5. Select best checkpoint by validation loss
516	      6. Return SFTResult
517	
518	    Args:
519	        config_path: Path to SFT YAML config.
520	        resume_from_checkpoint: Resume training from a checkpoint.
521	            - True: auto-detect the most recent checkpoint under output_dir.
522	            - str / Path: explicit checkpoint directory.
523	            - None / False (default): start fresh.
524	    """
525	    config = _load_sft_config(config_path)
526	    lora_cfg = config.get("lora", {})
527	    training_cfg = config.get("training", {})
528	    data_cfg = config.get("data", {})
529	    logging_cfg = config.get("logging", {})
530	
531	    loss_mask = training_cfg.get("loss_mask", _LOSS_MASK_ALL_TOKENS)
532	    if loss_mask not in _VALID_LOSS_MASKS:
533	        return SFTResult(
534	            error=(
535	                f"Unknown training.loss_mask={loss_mask!r}. "
536	                f"Valid values: {_VALID_LOSS_MASKS}."
537	            )
538	        )
539	    if loss_mask == _LOSS_MASK_RESPONSE_ONLY:
540	        # eval_loss averages over a different denominator under response_only
541	        # (only assistant tokens) vs all_tokens (every non-pad token), so the
542	        # two recipes' eval_loss numbers are not directly comparable. Within a
543	        # single run, metric_for_best_model: eval_loss still selects correctly.
544	        logger.warning(
545	            "sft_loss_mask_response_only",
546	            note=(
547	                "eval_loss is NOT comparable across loss_mask recipes; "
548	                "rank recipes via eval/agent_benchmark.py weighted_workflow_score."
549	            ),

555

558	
559	    with open(model_config_path) as f:

568	    # `_grouped_mm` LoRA path that crashes on Gemma-4 26B-A4B.
569	    #
570	    # Resolution order (first non-empty wins). Per-model settings beat
571	    # per-category defaults so individual models can pin a framework

581	        or training_cfg.get("framework")

605	                dtype=None,

628	        # TRL + PEFT path. Use AutoProcessor when the checkpoint is multimodal

630	        # AutoTokenizer. Model goes through standard transformers; LoRA is

632	        import torch

634	
635	        try:
636	            from transformers import AutoProcessor
637	            tokenizer = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_name)
638	        except (ValueError, OSError, KeyError):

857	        # Some rows (tool replies, multimodal stubs) carry content as a dict

860	        if c is None:

867	    # prompt the benchmark sees. Existing SFT JSONL has stale enrichment
868	    # baked in (broken workflow_script + old FORMAT_RULES); force_rebuild=True

871	    from llm_workflow_agents.data.system_prompt import build_enriched_system_prompt
872	
873	    def _load_split(name: str) -> Dataset:
874	        path = Path(data_source) / f"{name}.jsonl"
875	        if not path.exists():
876	            raise FileNotFoundError(f"SFT split missing: {path}")
877	        rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
878	        with open(path) as fh:
879	            for line in fh:
880	                if not line.strip():

883	                raw_msgs = raw.get("messages", []) or []

885	                if raw_msgs and raw_msgs[0].get("role") == "system" and raw.get("workflow_graph"):

891	                        ),
892	                    }

894	                    {
895	                        "role": m.get("role", "") or "",
896	                        "content": _coerce_content(m.get("content")),
897	                    }
898	                    for m in raw_msgs
899	                ]

902	            raise ValueError(f"SFT split is empty: {path}")

905	    # Render chat template AND pre-tokenize. TRL 0.23 + transformers 5.7's
906	    # SFTTrainer no longer auto-tokenizes a `text` column reliably under
907	    # Unsloth's wrapper — the default collator ends up trying to pad raw
